[[Malon engineer 001|Malon Engineer]] |image2 = Lower Decks cast.jpg |caption2 = Enberg with "Lower Decks" cast members Patti Yasutake, Bruce Beatty, Shannon Fill, and Dan Gauthier }}__NOTOC__ '''Alexander Philip Enberg''' {{born|5|April|1972}} is the actor best known to ''[[Star Trek]]'' [[Trekkie|fans]] for his [[VOY recurring characters#Vorik|recurring role]] as [[Ensign]] [[Vorik]] on {{s|VOY}}. Enberg is the son of {{s|TNG}} and ''Voyager'' producer and writer [[Jeri Taylor]] and sportscaster {{w|Dick Enberg}} and made his first ''Trek'' appearance in the ''Next Generation'' [[TNG Season 6|sixth season]] episode "[[Time's Arrow, Part II (episode)|Time's Arrow, Part II"]]. In the [[TNG Season 7|seventh season]] episode "[[Lower Decks (episode)|Lower Decks]]", Enberg portrayed the Vulcan Ensign [[Taurik]]. [[File:Shooting Blood Fever.jpg|thumb|left|Enberg with director [[Andrew Robinson]] on the set of "Blood Fever"]] For his first appearance as Vorik in the ''Star Trek: Voyager'' episode "[[Alter Ego (episode)|Alter Ego]]", Enberg is listed as "Alex Enberg" on the call sheets and filmed his scenes on Tuesday {{d|1|October|1996}} and Tuesday {{d|8|October|1996}} on [[Paramount Stage 9]] and [[Paramount Stage 16|16]] with makeup calls at 4:15/9:45 am and set calls at 7:30 am/12:15 pm. For the following episode "[[Fair Trade (episode)|Fair Trade]]", he filmed his scenes between Friday {{d|11|October|1996}} and Tuesday {{d|15|October|1996}} on [[Paramount Stage 8]] and 9. For his third appearance in the third season episode "[[Blood Fever (episode)|Blood Fever]]", Enberg filmed his scenes between Tuesday {{d|22|October|1996}} and Thursday {{d|24|October|1996}} and on Wednesday {{d|30|October|1996}} on Paramount Stage 9 and 16. For the fourth season episode "[[Day of Honor (episode)|Day of Honor]]", he filmed his scenes on Tuesday {{d|1|July|1997}} and Wednesday {{d|2|July|1997}} on Paramount Stage 9 with makeup calls at 4:30/5:15 am and set calls at 7:30/8:30 am. For "[[Demon (episode)|Demon]]", he filmed his scenes on the first day of production, Friday {{d|6|February|1998}} on Paramount Stage with a makeup call at 8:15 am and a set call at 12:00 noon. For the fifth season episode "Extreme Risk", Enberg filmed his scenes on Wednesday {{d|1|July|1998}} on Paramount Stage 16 with a makeup call at 4:15 am and a set call at 7:30 am. For the episode "Counterpoint", he filmed his scene on Monday {{d|14|September|1998}} on Paramount Stage 9 with a makeup call at 7:30 am and a set call at 11:00 am. According to the call sheets of the seventh season episode "Renaissance Man", Enberg was originally not planned to reprise his role as Vorik as he was not featured on them. His Starfleet uniforms from his portrayal of Vorik were later sold off on the [[It's A Wrap! sale and auction]] on eBay. {{stala|1986}} {{stala|6029}} {{stala|7033}} == Outside ''Star Trek'' == Early in his career, Enberg was featured in episodes of {{wt|Quincy, M.E.}} (1982 and 1983, starring [[Garry Walberg]], [[John S. Ragin]] and [[Robert Ito]] and with [[Renée Jones]]), {{wt|Simon & Simon}} (1987, with [[Mary Carver]], [[Ken Olandt]], [[Richard Gilbert-Hill]] and [[Conrad Hurtt]]), and {{wt|Jake and the Fatman}} (1990, with [[Cassandra Byram]]). On the first two series, his mother worked as executive story editor and on the last one as executive producer. Enberg was featured in {{wt|Pump Up the Volume (film)|Pump Up the Volume}} (1990, starring [[Christian Slater]], with [[Robert Schenkkan]], [[Gregg Daniel]], [[Clayton Landey]], [[John Kenton Shull]] and [[Ed Trotta]]) and had guest roles in episodes of {{wt|Father Dowling Mysteries}} (1991, with [[Eugene Roche]] and [[Roger Aaron Brown]]), ''Blossom'' (1992), {{wt|Knots Landing}} (1992, with [[Peter Slutsker]] and directed by [[Reza Badiyi]]), {{wt|Step by Step (TV series)|Step by Step}} (1993, with [[David Graf]]), {{wt|Lois & Clark: The New Adventures of Superman}} (1993, starring [[Teri Hatcher]], [[K Callan]] and [[Tracy Scoggins]], with Gregg Daniel), and ''Dead at 21'' (1994). In 1994, Enberg appeared in and worked as producer on the action drama ''The Source of Suction'', with [[Tory Christopher]] and [[Shannon Fill]]. He also appeared in {{wt|Junior (1994 film)|Junior}} (1994, with [[Frank Langella]], [[Stefan Gierasch]], [[Lawrence Tierney]], [[Ethan Dampf]] and [[Tracey Walter]]), [[Scott McGinnis]]' thriller ''Last Gasp'' (1995, with [[Vyto Ruginis]], [[Nan Martin]] and [[Ed Anders]]), and the television series {{wt|Get Smart (1995 TV series)|Get Smart}} (1995, with [[Andy Dick]]) and {{wt|Murder One (TV series)|Murder One}} (1997, with [[Barbara Bosson]], [[Clayton Rohner]], [[Jack Kehler]], [[Dennis Creaghan]], [[Ellen Albertini Dow]], [[John Fleck]], [[Jack Blessing]], [[Richard McGonagle]], [[Victor Bevine]] and producer and director [[Marc Buckland]]). Further acting work include {{wt|Gia}} (1998, with [[Joan Pringle]], [[Louis Giambalvo]], [[Shelby Leverington]], [[Tricia O'Neil]] and [[Paul Sandman]]), {{wt|Senseless}} (1998, with [[Jenette Goldstein]], [[Richard McGonagle]], [[Greg Grunberg]], [[Brad Dourif]], [[Manu Intiraymi]], [[Ivar Brogger]], [[Cyia Batten]], [[Jack Shearer]], [[Len Costanza]], [[John Wilkie]], [[Janet Dey]], [[Rubin Knight]], [[Andray Johnson]] and [[Bruce Dobos]]), episodes of ''NYPD Blue'' (1998, with [[Gordon Clapp]], [[Sharon Lawrence]] and [[Aaron Lustig]]), {{wt|V.I.P. (American TV series)|V.I.P.}} (1998, with [[John Cho]]), {{wt|Zoe, Duncan, Jack and Jane}} (1999), and ''The Invisible Man'' (2001, with Ivar Brogger), {{wt|Pirates of Silicon Valley}} (1999, with [[J.G. Hertzler]], [[Nikita Ager]], [[Jeffrey Nordling]], [[Wayne Péré]], [[Clay Wilcox]], [[Paul Popowich]], [[Allan G. Royal]], [[Karl Wiedergott]], [[Kitty Swink]] and [[Marc Worden]]), {{wt|America's Sweethearts}} (2001, with [[Christopher Walken]], [[Rainn Wilson]], [[Wendy Schenker]] and [[Ann Cusack]]), {{wt|Surviving Gilligan's Island}} (2001, with Aaron Lustig, [[Steve Vinovich]], [[Christopher Neiman]], [[Ray Buktenica]] and [[James W. Jansen]]), and the thriller ''Panic'' (2002, with [[Kristanna Loken]], [[Tucker Smallwood]] and [[David Bowe]]). Enberg later worked as special effects artist on the ''Howard Stern on Demand'' segment "Fartman: Caught in a Tight Ass" (2006) and on the comedy ''Never Say Macbeth'' (2007, with [[Melodee Spevack]] and [[Sam Zeller]]). On the latter project he also worked as actor and as additional editor. He made his directing debut with the comedy ''Searching for Ron Ficus'' in 2009 on which he also worked as visual effects artist and worked as visual effects artist on the comedy ''Desperate Acts of Magic'' (2013). In 2013, Enberg suffered from a serious stroke but has since recovered. {{el|gaslampball.com/2013/5/30/4380276/dick-enberg-tending-to-serious-family-medical-issue}} {{el|chrisreblogs.tumblr.com/post/51853175196/this-is-a-bit-weird-to-post-but-i-am-going-to}} {{twitter|schnarr84/status/488851837638828032}} He formed a musical act named Survivors' Cabaret with cancer survivor and fellow ''Star Trek'' alum [[Kendra Munger]], which became the subject of a documentary. {{el|trekbbs.com/threads/short-documentary-on-alex-enberg-taurik-from-tng-and-vorik-from-voyager.300453/#post-13014394}} {{el|challenge.musicbed.com/submissions/survivors-cabaret/DbAg1G}} == ''Star Trek'' appearances == File:San Francisco reporter.jpg|[[Human 19th century young reporter|Young Reporter]]

'''Robert Bauer''' is the actor, musician, writer, and producer who portrayed [[Kunivas]] in the {{s|TNG}} [[TNG Season 1|first season]] episode {{e|Heart of Glory}}. Footage of this appearance was later re-used in the [[TNG Season 2|second season]] episode {{e|Shades of Gray}}.

Bauer is a professional drummer who used to play in the band "The Watch" in which fellow ''The Next Generation'' co-star [[Michael Dorn]] played the bass. Bauer is probably best known for his portrayal of Johnny Horne, the mentally ill older brother of actress {{w|Sherilyn Fenn}} in {{wt|Twin Peaks}}. Bauer also filmed scene for {{wt|Twin Peaks: Fire Walk with Me}} in 1992 but his scenes were deleted. On ''Twin Peaks'' he worked with ''Trek'' alumni [[Mädchen Amick]], [[Richard Beymer]], [[Ray Wise]], [[Sheryl Lee]], [[Miguel Ferrer]], [[Wendy Robie]], [[Michael John Anderson]], [[Catherine Coulson]], [[Kenneth Welsh]], [[David Warner]] and [[Brenda Strong]]. Following ''Twin Peaks'', Bauer and friend and actor {{w|Dana Ashbrook}}, brother of [[Daphne Ashbrook]], founded the film company "Bauerbrook Films".

Among his first film roles are parts in {{wt|Desperate Characters (film)|Desperate Characters}} (1971, with [[Kenneth Mars]] and [[Carol Kane]]), {{wt|This Is Spinal Tap}} (1984, with [[Michael McKean]] and [[Ed Begley, Jr.]]), and {{wt|The Sure Thing}} (1985, with [[John Putch]], [[Larry A. Hankin]], and [[Christopher Rydell]]).

Following his appearance on ''Star Trek'', Bauer had featured parts in {{wt|The Big Picture (1989 film)|The Big Picture}} (1989, with Michael McKean, [[Teri Hatcher]], [[Stephen Collins]], and [[Stan Ivar]]), the television drama ''Parker Kane'' (1990, with [[William Lucking]], [[Henry Kingi, Sr.]], [[James Ingersoll]] and [[Todd Feder]]), {{wt|Father of the Bride (1991 film)|Father of the Bride}} (1991, with [[Frank Kopyc]]), {{wt|Something to Live for: The Alison Gertz Story}} (1992, starring [[Martin Landau]], with [[George Coe]], [[Janet MacLachlan]], [[Victor Brandt]],  [[Neil C. Vipond]] and [[Ren Hanami]]), and in the television production ''A Spinal Tap Reunion: The 25th Anniversary London Sell-Out'' (1992, with Michael McKean). He also had guest parts in episodes of {{wt|Living Dolls}} (1989), ''Father Dowling Mysteries'' (1991, with [[Stanley Kamel]], [[Richard Riehle]], [[Debi A. Monahan]], and [[David Anthony Marshall]]), {{wt|Quantum Leap (1989 TV series)|Quantum Leap}} (1991, starring [[Scott Bakula]] and [[Dean Stockwell]]), and {{wt|In Living Color}} (1991).

Between 1992 and 1993 he portrayed the recurring character Jordan in {{wt|Flying Blind (TV series)|Flying Blind}}. The series also featured [[Cristine Rose]], [[Charles Rocket]] and [[Aaron Lustig]]. Further credits include {{wt|Boogie Boy}} (1998, with [[Karen Sheperd]], [[Phil Culotta]], and [[James Lew]]), {{wt|54 (film)|54}} (1998, with [[Ellen Albertini Dow]]), the comedy ''Dirk and Betty'' (1999, with [[Pamela Segall]]), {{wt|Intrepid (film)|Intrepid}} (2000, with [[Kevin Rahm]], [[Johnny Martin]], [[Clive Revill]] and [[Warren Munson]]), and {{wt|A Time to Remember (film)|A Time to Remember}} (2003, with [[Megan Gallagher]], [[Louise Fletcher]], [[Rosemary Forsyth]] and [[Erich Anderson]]). Bauer also had guest roles in episodes of {{wt|NYPD Blue}} (1994, with [[Gordon Clapp]], [[Sharon Lawrence]] and [[Jack Shearer]]), {{wt|M.A.N.T.I.S.}} (1994, starring [[Galyn Görg]], with [[Malachi Throne]]), {{wt|Party of Five}} (1995, with [[Scott Grimes]] and [[Angela Dohrmann]]), {{wt|Sabrina the Teenage Witch (1996 TV series)|Sabrina the Teenage Witch}} (1999), {{wt|Yes, Dear}} (2000, with [[Don Most]] and [[Michael Owen]]), and ''The Lot'' (2001, with [[Tami-Adrian George]], [[Jonathan Frakes]], and [[Kim Rhodes]]).

Since 1990, he has also worked as producer on projects such as the short drama ''Marilyn Hotchkiss' Ballroom Dancing and Charm School'' (1990), the short film ''Waiting for Woody'' (1998, with Pamela Adlon), his directorial debut ''Dirk and Betty'' (1990), the short comedy ''The Ingrate'' (2004), and {{wt|Waitress (2007 film)|Waitress}} (2007, starring [[Keri Russell]]). In 2007 he and Alexandra Wentworth created {{wt|Head Case}} (2007-09) which ran for three seasons and on which he also worked as Executive Producer, Writer, and Unit Production Manager.

In a [[StarTrek.com]] interview, she mentions that she married her {{e|Defiant}} co-star Canavan, and that he was the only person, aside from [[Jonathan Frakes]] and [[Nana Visitor]], she filmed the episode with. Her makeup artist for this episode was [[Dean Gates]]. Cochran has guest-starred in episodes of {{wt|ER (TV series)|ER}}, ''[[Frasier]]'' (2003, starring [[Kelsey Grammer]], with [[John Vickery]]), {{wt|NYPD Blue}}, {{wt|Seinfeld}}, ''Full House'', and {{wt|The Office (American TV series)|The Office}} (2005, starring [[Rainn Wilson]]). She had earlier worked with her on-screen husband [[J.G. Hertzler]] in the "Treasure Island" show at the Treasure Island Hotel in Las Vegas (the same film also starred [[Anthony Zerbe]]). Cochran is probably best known for her role as Anna Morgan in {{wt|The Ring (2002 film)|The Ring}} (2002, with [[Richard Lineback]], [[Joe Chrest]], [[Stephanie Erb]], [[Lindsey Stoddart]], [[Keith Campbell]], [[Chuck Hicks]], and [[Michael Spound]]). Abrams]]' {{wt|Fringe (TV series)|Fringe}} (2010, starring [[Joshua Jackson]] and [[John Noble]]), ''Off the Map'' (2011), {{wt|Desperate Housewives}} (2011, with [[Teri Hatcher]], [[Vanessa Williams]], [[Brenda Strong]], [[Mark Moses]], and [[Kevin Rahm]]), {{wt|Scandal (TV series)|Scandal}} (2012-13, with [[Mark Harelik]]), {{wt|NCIS (TV series)|NCIS}} (2014), and {{wt|NCIS: Los Angeles}} (2015, with [[Miguel Ferrer]]). '''Tracy Middendorf''' {{born|26|January|1970}} is an actress who played [[Tora Ziyal]] in the {{s|DS9}} [[DS9 Season 4|fourth season]] episode {{e|For the Cause}}. As revealed in ''[[Cinefantastique]]'' (Vol. 28, No. 4/5, p. 63), Middendorf also [[Performers considered for DS9 roles|auditioned for the role]] of [[Mardah]], prior to portraying Ziyal.

Born in Miami Beach, Florida, Middendorf was in her senior year at Pickens High School in Jasper, Georgia when, in 1987, she left to enter a performing arts school in Miami. She later attended the State University of New York (SUNY) at Purchase. 

In 1992, she won the role of Carrie Brady (another character who has been played by three actresses) on {{wt|Days of Our Lives}}, which had also starred [[John de Lancie]]. The following year, she began playing the recurring role of Laura Kingman during the fourth season of {{wt|Beverly Hills, 90210}}. In 1994, she made her film debut with a supporting role in {{wt|Wes Craven's New Nightmare}}, starring [[Robert Englund]] and [[Heather Langenkamp]], with [[Fran Bennett]], [[Cully Fredricksen]] and [[Matt Winston]].

In the first ten years of her career, she was seen in such television dramas as {{wt|Murder, She Wrote}} (1996, with fellow ''Deep Space Nine'' guest-stars [[Richard Beymer]], [[Meg Foster]] and [[Richard Libertini]]), {{wt|Touched by an Angel}} (1997, written by [[Ken LaZebnik]] and co-starring [[Clive Revill]]), {{wt|L.A. Doctors}} (1998, starring [[Sheryl Lee]], with [[John Billingsley]]), {{wt|Ally McBeal}} (two 1999 episodes, including one with [[Albert Hall]] and [[Ray Walston]]), {{wt|Family Law (American TV series)|Family Law}} (with [[Scott MacDonald]], [[Christopher McDonald]] and [[Julie Warner]]), {{wt|Six Feet Under (TV series)|Six Feet Under}} (with [[Ed Begley, Jr.]]), {{wt|JAG (TV series)|JAG}} (with [[Zach Grenier]], [[Scott Lawrence]] and [[Terry O'Quinn]]), and {{wt|Any Day Now (TV series)|Any Day Now}} (with [[Daniel Dae Kim]] and [[Tom Wright]]). She also had a recurring role on {{wt|The Practice}}, working with [[Bruce Davison]], [[Bruce French]], [[John Larroquette]], [[Richard McGonagle]], [[Lawrence Pressman]] and [[Steve Rankin]].

Middendorf's subsequent science fiction credits following her appearance on ''Deep Space Nine'' include an episode of ''Perversions of Science'' with [[Chris Sarandon]], the first episode of {{wt|Angel (1999 TV series)|Angel}} (1999, with [[Vyto Ruginis]]) and an episode of ''[[The X-Files]]'' (2000, starring [[Gillian Anderson]], with [[Randy Oglesby]]). Her later TV work included four episodes of {{wt|24 (TV series)|24}} (2002, with [[Michelle Forbes]], [[Penny Johnson]], [[Timothy Carhart]], [[Jude Ciccolella]], [[Harris Yulin]], [[Tamlyn Tomita]], [[Jimmi Simpson]] and [[Billy Burke]]) and guest spots on {{wt|CSI: Crime Scene Investigation}} (2003 & 2009, starring [[Paul Guilfoyle]], former with [[Leslie Silva]], latter co-starring [[Wallace Langham]] and [[Liz Vassey]]), {{wt|Cold Case}} (with [[Michael Nouri]]), {{wt|Medical Investigation}} (2004, starring [[Neal McDonough]] and [[Christopher Gorham]], with [[Patrick Fabian]] and [[Kristen Ariza]]), {{wt|House (TV series)|House}} (with [[Jennifer Morrison]]), {{wt|Without a Trace}} (2006, starring [[Enrique Murciano]] and [[Eric Close]], with [[Jane Daly]], [[Rebecca Wisocky]] and [[John de Lancie]]), {{wt|Shark (American TV series)|Shark}} (starring [[Jeri Ryan]], with [[Billy Campbell]], [[Graham Shiels]] and [[Ivar Brogger]]), and {{wt|Law & Order: Special Victims Unit}} (2007, starring [[Mariska Hargitay]], with [[Steven Weber]]). 

Middendorf has worked with [[J.J. Abrams]] several times. She appeared in two episodes of Abrams' {{wt|Alias (TV series)|Alias}} in 2003 starring [[Merrin Dungey]] and [[Victor Garber]], with [[Terry O'Quinn]] and [[Greg Grunberg]] in the first, [[William Dennis Hunt]] in the second, and [[Christian Slater]] in both. The first of those were written by [[Alex Kurtzman]] and [[Roberto Orci]] and directed by the latter. Three years later, Middendorf appeared in Abrams' feature film directorial debut, [[Paramount Pictures]]' {{wt|Mission: Impossible III}} (2006, also co-written by Kurtzman and Orci and co-starring [[Simon Pegg]] and Greg Grunberg). Middendorf also appeared in two episodes of {{wt|Lost (TV series)|Lost}}, co-created by Abrams and [[Damon Lindelof]] and starring [[Naveen Andrews]], Daniel Dae Kim, Terry O'Quinn and [[Sam Anderson]].

Middendorf has also guest starred in {{wt|Boardwalk Empire}}, {{wt|Scream (TV series)|Scream}}, and {{wt|The Last Ship (TV series)|The Last Ship}}.

'''Mary Crosby''' {{born|14|September|1959}} is the actress who played [[Natima Lang]] in the {{s|DS9}} [[DS9 Season 2|second season]] episode {{e|Profit and Loss}}.

She is the daughter of singer {{w|Bing Crosby}} and actress Kathryn Crosby. She is also the aunt of {{s|TNG}} actress [[Denise Crosby]], although she is  two years younger.

== Early life and career ==
Crosby was born in Los Angeles, California. She began acting when she was six years old, appearing in a Bay Area stage production of ''Peter Pan'' with her mother. She made her television debut when she was eight years old, appearing with her father and [[Joan Collins]] in an episode of ''The Danny Thomas Hour''. She continued appearing with her father and other family members on a number of Christmas television specials throughout the 1970s.

She graduated from high school at the age of 15 and enrolled at the University of Texas at Austin, but dropped out before graduating. She then auditioned for San Francisco's American Conservatory Theatre (ACT), becoming the youngest person to be accepted by the repertory at the time. It was while at ACT rehearsing for a production of ''Julius Caesar'' that, on 14 October 1977, Crosby learned of her famous father's death of a heart attack at the age of 74.

Crosby began acting on television professionally in 1978, appearing on {{wt|Starsky & Hutch}} (starring [[David Soul]], in an episode directed by [[Reza Badiyi]]) and {{wt|CHiPs}} (starring [[Robert Pine]]). She also played Patricia North in {{wt|Pearl (miniseries)|Pearl}} (1978, with [[Gregg Henry]], [[Charles Lucia]] and [[Allan Miller]]).

In early 1979, Crosby was a regular on [[NBC]]'s {{wt|Brothers and Sisters (1979 TV series)|Brothers and Sisters}}. On this series, Crosby played Suzi Cooper, was a member of the Gamma Iota sorority at Larry Krandall College. The college is founded and run by its namesake, played by [[William Windom]]. [[Larry Anderson]] was also part of the cast. After ''Brothers and Sisters'' bombed, Crosby found some difficulty in finding another acting job on television.

== ''Dallas'' ==
Crosby is perhaps best remembered for playing the scheming Kristin Shepard on [[CBS Studios|CBS]]' {{wt|Dallas (TV series)|Dallas}}. She joined the series in 1979 and remained through 1981. It was her character who shot J.R. Ewing in the cliffhanger ending of the 1979-1980 season; this revelation came in the November 1980 episode "Who Done It?", which was the highest-rated program in television history at the time and remains the second most-watched television episode in the United States.

During her time on ''Dallas'', Crosby worked with many other ''Star Trek'' alumni, including [[Barbara Babcock]], [[Michael Bell]], [[Ellen Bry]], [[Nicolas Coster]], [[Walker Edmiston]], [[Stefan Gierasch]], [[Susan Howard]], [[Leigh J. McCloskey]], [[William Smithers]], [[Paul Sorensen]] and [[Morgan Woodward]]. [[Joshua Harris]] played her character's biological son Christopher Ewing on the series. Crosby also played Kristin in a 1980 episode of the ''Dallas'' spin-off, {{wt|Knots Landing}}.

She returned to the role of Kristin for ''Dallas''{{'}} series finale in 1991, appearing in a "dream" sequence in which J.R. sees what life would be like if he had never been born. The "dream" was presented by an "angel" played by {{s|VOY}} guest star [[Joel Grey]], who ultimately coerced J.R. to (apparently) commit suicide by shooting himself. As such, two characters played by ''Star Trek'' veterans were responsible for J.R. getting shot.

== After ''Dallas'' ==
After leaving ''Dallas'', Crosby appeared in a pilot for ABC called ''Golden Gate'', in which Crosby, [[Jean Simmons]] and [[Richard Kiley]] played members of the Kingsley family. [[Jason Evers]], [[Don Keefer]], [[Warren Munson]] and ''Voyager''{{'}}s [[Robert Picardo]] also appeared in the movie.

Crosby made her film debut in {{wt|Last Plane Out}} (1983), for which she reunited with her ''Brothers and Sisters'' co-star, William Windom. She also appeared with Windom in an episode of ''Automan'' that same year, along with [[Robert Lansing]], who was a regular on that series.

Perhaps Crosby's best-known film role is that of Prince Karina in {{wt|The Ice Pirates}} (1984, with [[Ron Perlman]], [[Robert Symonds]] and [[Ian Abercrombie]]). In 1988, Crosby starred in {{wt|Tapeheads}} (1988, featuring [[Lee Arenberg]]).

Crosby portrayed Isabel Hazard in the epic 1986 mini-series ''North and South, Book II''. Her character was the wife of Stanley Hazard, played by ''The Next Generation''{{'}}s [[Jonathan Frakes]]; her character's sister-in-law, Virgilia, was played by {{film|2}} actress [[Kirstie Alley]] and her brother-in-law, George, was played by ''Voyager'' guest actor [[James Read]]. Other ''Star Trek'' alumni who worked on this production include [[Michael Champion]], [[Jim Metzler]], [[Bumper Robinson]], [[William Schallert]], Jean Simmons, [[Kurtwood Smith]], [[David Ogden Stiers]] and [[Anthony Zerbe]].

Throughout the 1980s, Crosby made multiple appearances on {{wt|The Fall Guy}}, {{wt|The Love Boat}}, and ''Hotel''. She also appeared on ''Finder of Lost Loves'' with [[Michelle Phillips]] in 1984, starred with [[Joanna Cassidy]] in {{wt|Hollywood Wives (miniseries)|Hollywood Wives}} (1985), and appeared with [[Merritt Butrick]] in {{wt|Stagecoach (1986 film)|Stagecoach}} (1986). In 1987, she guest-starred in the series premiere of ''The New Adventures of Beans Baxter'', which starred [[Elinor Donahue]] and Kurtwood Smith.

Crosby continued acting on stage, as well. She played Juliet in a 1985 Los Angeles production of [[William Shakespeare]]'s ''[[Romeo and Juliet]]'', for which she acted alongside [[James Cromwell]]. She returned to the role for another LA production of the play in 1988, earning praise and a Drama-Logue Award for her performance. She then performed in the Los Angeles Theater Company's production of ''The Seagull'', which ran from 1988 through 1989.

In 1989, Crosby filmed two appearances on {{wt|Freddy's Nightmares}} (one of which aired in January 1990). In the first episode, "Lucky Stiff", Crosby and [[David L. Lander]] played a married couple; after Lander's character dies, Crosby realizes he purchased a winning lottery ticket, but it may have been buried with him. [[Tracey Walter]] played a grave digger who resorts to blackmail to win the woman of his dreams. In the follow-up episode, "Easy Come, Easy Go", Crosby and Walter's characters are married, with Crosby planning to murder Walter.

== 1990-present ==
Crosby appeared in several films during the 1990s. She was seen in four films in 1990 alone, three of which co-starred other ''Star Trek'' performers: ''Deadly Innocents'' with {{dis|John Anderson|actor}}, {{wt|Body Chemistry (1990 film)|Body Chemistry}} with [[David Kagen]], and {{wt|Corporate Affairs}} with [[Richard Herd]]. In 1992, she worked with [[Stephen Davies]] in the action film ''The Berlin Conspiracy''. She then starred with [[Brian Bonsall]] in the 1993 thriller film ''Distant Cousins''.

On television, Crosby appeared in two episodes of {{wt|Murder, She Wrote}}, the first of which was directed by [[Vincent McEveety]] and co-starred [[Gary Lockwood]]. The second episode again saw Crosby acting with William Windom. They worked together one last time in a 1995 episode of ''Burke's Law'', along with [[Michael Nouri]] and ''Deep Space Nine'' regular [[Nana Visitor]].

Crosby also guest-starred on such television series as {{wt|Paradise (1988 TV series)|Paradise}} (with [[David Graf]]), {{wt|Lois & Clark: The New Adventures of Superman}} (starring [[Teri Hatcher]], [[K Callan]] and [[Tracy Scoggins]], with [[Roy Brocksmith]], [[Tony Jay]]), and {{wt|Orleans (TV series)|Orleans}} (with [[Michael Reilly Burke]], [[Jerry Hardin]] and [[J. Patrick McNamara]]). In addition, she played the recurring role of Claudia Van Eyck on {{wt|Beverly Hills, 90210}}, working with [[Stanley Kamel]].

In the 1997 horror film ''Cupid'', Crosby and [[Zach Galligan]] play two murderous, incestuous siblings. In 2000, Crosby worked with [[Lawrence Monoson]] in the TV movie ''Sharing the Secret''. In 2005, she played Governor Riley' wife in ''The Legend of Zorro'' (2005), which was written by [[Roberto Orci]] and [[Alex Kurtzman]].

Since ''The Legend of Zorro'', Crosby has only appeared in three films, all written and directed by British-American playwright and actor {{w|Henry Jaglom}}. ''Queen of the Lot'' (2010, with [[Christopher Rydell]], [[Dennis Christopher]], [[Diane Salinger]] and [[Phil Proctor]]), ''Just 45 Minutes from Broadway'' (2012, with Diane Salinger and [[Jack Quaid]]), and ''The M Word'' (2014), the latter being her last screen credit to date.

'''William Lucking''' {{born|17|June|1941|died|18|October|2021}} was the actor who played [[Furel]] in the {{s|DS9}} episodes {{e|The Darkness and the Light}} and {{e|Ties of Blood and Water}}, and [[Harrad-Sar]] in the {{s|ENT}} [[ENT Season 4|fourth season]] episode {{e|Bound}}. He filmed his scenes for this on Friday {{d|14|January|2005}}.

Lucking was a seasoned veteran film, television, and stage actor perhaps best known for his role as Piney Winston in {{wt|Sons of Anarchy}}.

== Biography ==
=== Film and television ===
Lucking's imposing figure and rough-hewn features lent themselves well to roles as tough bikers (''Hell's Belles'', ''Wild Rovers'', ''Sons of Anarchy''), craggy cowboys (''The Magnificent Seven Ride!'', ''The Return of a Man Called Horse''), and determined military and police officers (''Doc Savage: The Man of Bronze'', ''K-PAX''). His film work also includes appearances in {{wt|10 (1979 film)|10}} (1979), {{wt|The Mountain Men}} (1980), {{wt|Stripes (film)|Stripes}} (1981), {{wt|Ladykillers (film)|Ladykillers}} (1988), {{wt|The River Wild}} (1994), {{wt|The Limey}} (1999), {{wt|Erin Brockovich (film)|Erin Brockovich}} (2000), {{wt|Red Dragon (2002 film)|Red Dragon}} (2002), {{wt|The Rundown}}, and {{wt|Contraband (2012 film)|Contraband}} (2012).

On television he had a featured role in {{wt|Outlaws (1986 TV series)|Outlaws}} as Harland Pike. He was a mainstay on episodic TV for three decades, appearing in such classics as ''[[Mission: Impossible]]'', {{wt|The Partridge Family}}, {{wt|Simon & Simon}}, {{wt|Bonanza}}, {{wt|Kung Fu (1972 TV series)|Kung Fu}} (1973, with [[Gregory Sierra]], [[Ike Eisenmann]], [[Keye Luke]] and [[Brian Tochi]]), {{wt|Gunsmoke}}, {{wt|The Rockford Files}}, {{wt|The Waltons}}, {{wt|The Incredible Hulk (1978 TV series)|The Incredible Hulk}}, {{wt|M*A*S*H (TV series)|M*A*S*H}}, {{wt|Knight Rider (1982 TV series)|Knight Rider}}, {{wt|Magnum, P.I.}} (1983, with [[Matthew Faison]]), {{wt|Hunter (1984 American TV series)|Hunter}}, and ''The Greatest American Hero''. He also appeared in such shows as {{wt|JAG (TV series)|JAG}}, {{wt|Walker, Texas Ranger}}, ''[[The X-Files]]'', {{wt|ER (TV series)|ER}}, {{wt|The Pretender (TV series)|The Pretender}}, {{wt|Profiler (TV series)|Profiler}}, {{wt|The West Wing}}, {{wt|Tales of the Gold Monkey}} and ''In the Heat of the Night''.

He starred as Colonel Lynch in {{wt|The A-Team}}, which also featured [[Dwight Schultz]], [[Lance LeGault]], and [[Melinda Culea]]. He also guest-starred in {{wt|NYPD Blue}} (1995, starring [[Gordon Clapp]] and [[Sharon Lawrence]], with [[Michael Reilly Burke]], [[Kavi Raz]], [[Bill Bolender]] and [[Angela Paton]]), {{wt|Murder, She Wrote}}, {{wt|Millennium (TV series)|Millennium}}, and {{wt|Cold Case}}, with [[Nicolas Coster]], [[Conor O'Farrell]], and [[Leon Russom]]. He portrayed Piermont 'Piney' Winston on {{wt|Sons of Anarchy}} from 2008-2011.

Lucking's film performances include {{wt|Stripes (film)|Stripes}} (1981, with Lance LeGault and [[John Larroquette]]), and {{wt|The Rundown}} (2003, starring [[The Rock]] and [[Christopher Walken]]).

=== Theatre ===
Lucking graduated from UCLA and the Pasadena Playhouse with degrees in literature and theatre. In 1986, with fellow actor and Michigan native Dana Elcar, he co-founded the Santa Paula Theater Center.

As co-instructor of the company's free acting workshop he was admired for his minimalist approach; a counterpoint to Elcar's methodical style. He served alongside Elcar as artistic director for five seasons. He was Producer of projects including Edward Albee's ''The Zoo Story'', Harold Pinter's ''The Hothouse'', George Bernard Shaw's ''Major Barbara'', Tennessee Williams' {{wt|Camino Real (play)|Camino Real}}, and Robert Penn Warren's ''All the King's Men''. Lucking's later roles include Blue in the CTG/Ahmanson production of ''Conversations with My Father'' at the Doolittle Theater in Los Angeles and Dr. Sloper in the Ensemble Theater Company of Santa Barbara's production of ''The Heiress''.

Wildman's most noteworthy television role is that of undercover FBI agent Christine Pettit on {{wt|Beverly Hills, 90210}}. Ostensibly, Pettit was the girlfriend of Jack McKay played by Josh Taylor whose ex-wife Iris was portrayed by [[Stephanie Beacham]]. Wildman was featured largely in the third season from 1992 to 1993. Her debut was that season's Thanksgiving-themed "The Kindness of Strangers" (1992) (with [[Clyde Kusatsu]] and [[Melanie Smith]]), then in 1993 was "Back in the High Life Again" (with [[Ann Gillespie]]), then "Dead End" (with Gillespie again) in which Pettit was revealed to be a federal law enforcement officer; her final appearance that season was "The Child is Father to the Man" (directed by [[James Whitmore, Jr.]], with [[Miguel Perez]]). Wildman resumed playing Pettit in the fifth season in the holiday episode "Christmas Comes This Time Each Year" (1994, with Beacham as well as [[Michael Durrell]]) and "P.S. I Love You Too" (1995, directed by [[Victor Lobl]]). In 2000, Wildman returned in the tenth and final season as Pettit resurfaced in "Eddie Waitkus" (directed by [[Chip Chalmers]]) and finally "Ever Heard the One About the Exploding Father?" (directed by [[Anson Williams]], and with [[Matt Winston]]).

===21st century work===
Wildman's first film in this century was {{wt|Crime and Punishment in Suburbia}} (2000, with [[Brad Greenquist]] and [[Marshall R. Teague]]), {{wt|Cast Away}} (2000, starring [[Tom Hanks]], with [[Jenifer Lewis]], [[Michael Forest]] and [[Nan Martin]]). Wildman got her first telefilm role of the decade in ''Mystery Woman'' (2003, with [[David Bowe]] and [[Clarence Williams III]]) and was later in {{wt|Nip/Tuck}} (2003, with [[Don McManus]] and [[Brenda Strong]]).

Wildman later worked again with ''Beverly Hills Cop II'' producer Jerry Bruckhemier on {{wt|CSI: Crime Scene Investigation}} (2005, starring Paul Guilfoyle and [[Wallace Langham]], with Nan Martin, [[Wendie Malick]] and [[Greg Ellis]]), {{wt|Cold Case}} (2006, with fellow ''Voyager'' guest [[Tom Virtue]]) and {{wt|Without a Trace}} (starring [[Enrique Murciano]] and [[Eric Close]], with [[David Doty]]). Wildman then appeared in {{wt|The Last Sin Eater (film)|The Last Sin Eater}} (2007, starring [[Louise Fletcher]]).
